blocks.prompt: The Chest With the Secret Keyhole
blocks.text: People have kept treasure in chests for hundreds of years. A real treasure chest was not a toy. It was a heavy box of wood and iron. It sat in a shop or a strong room. Some were so heavy that four men could not lift one. The best chests had a trick. On the front was a keyhole. But that keyhole was fake. It did nothing at all. The real keyhole hid under a little flap in the lid. When you turned the true key, iron bolts shot out on every side at once. A thief could poke at the fake hole all night and never get in.

blocks.prompt: The Keyhole That Does Nothing
blocks.text: Think of a treasure chest and you probably picture a rounded wooden box full of gold, buried in the sand. Real treasure chests were nothing like that. The strongest ones were built in Germany, in towns called Nuremberg and Augsburg, about four hundred years ago. They were made of iron. They were plain and ugly and unbelievably heavy. A merchant kept one bolted to the floor of his counting room, and it held coins, contracts, and records. The clever part was the lock. Look at the front of one of these chests and you will find a keyhole. Try it. Nothing happens. It is a decoy, put there to waste a thief's time. The true keyhole sits in the middle of the lid, hidden under a flap that you have to know how to release. Turn the real key and the whole lid comes alive. Iron bolts shoot out of the lid into the frame on all four sides at the same moment. Nobody buried a chest like that. You would need six men and a cart just to move it.

blocks.prompt: The Fact That Ruins a Good Story
blocks.text: Here is a fact that ruins a good story. Pirates almost never buried treasure. Think about it from a pirate's side. A pirate crew was a business, and a violent, short-lived one. Most men expected to be caught or killed within a couple of years. Money buried in a hole is money you cannot spend, and it only works if you live long enough to come back for it, and if you can find the spot again, and if none of your shipmates dig it up first. So pirates did what people do when they think tomorrow is unlikely. They divided the loot immediately, by written agreement, and spent it in port. There is one famous exception, and it did not end well. In 1699, Captain William Kidd buried a share of his treasure on Gardiners Island, near New York, hoping to use it as a bargaining chip. He was arrested anyway. The governor's men dug the treasure straight back up, shipped it to England, and laid it out in court as evidence against him. Kidd was hanged in London in 1701. The one pirate who really did bury treasure was destroyed by it. Most pirate loot was not gold anyway. It was cargo: cloth, sugar, rope, tools, medicine, food, and spare sails. Boring, useful, and easy to sell. A chest of glittering coins makes a better picture than eleven barrels of cloth, so that is the picture we kept.

blocks.prompt: Where the X Came From
blocks.text: Every child can draw a treasure map. A curl of coastline, a palm tree, a dotted path, and an X where the gold waits. That image is not ancient. It is a piece of Victorian publishing, and we can name the man who drew it. In 1881, in a rented cottage in Scotland, Robert Louis Stevenson was entertaining his bored stepson on a wet afternoon. He drew an island. He named its bays and hills, added a few crosses to mark buried treasure, and, as he described it later, the characters began appearing on the page among the imaginary woods. The map came first. The novel came second. Treasure Island handed us nearly the whole pirate costume at once: the one-legged sea cook, the parrot on the shoulder, the black spot, pieces of eight, and above all the map. Writers had circled the idea before him, notably Edgar Allan Poe in The Gold-Bug in 1843, but Stevenson is the one who made it permanent. The real article is less romantic and more impressive. The finest strongboxes in Europe were hammered out in Nuremberg and Augsburg in the 1600s. Antique dealers now sell them as armada chests, which sounds like salt spray and cannon smoke, but most of them never went near a ship. They lived in counting houses and town treasuries, bolted to the floor, holding payroll and paperwork. Their genius is on the underside of the lid, where a mechanism as wide as the lid itself throws a dozen iron bolts into the frame at once. The keyhole on the front is a fake, a decoy left for thieves to work at all night. The one pirate ship we have actually found tells the same story. The Whydah went down in a storm off Cape Cod in 1717 and was located in 1984, the only pirate wreck ever authenticated, confirmed by its own inscribed bell. Divers brought up coins and gold dust, yes. They also brought up cannons, shoes, tools, buttons, and the leg bone of a child, because a boy somewhere between eight and eleven was serving in the crew. That is what a pirate ship really contained. So we have two chests. One is buried, marked with an X, and does not exist. The other is bolted to a floor in Germany, ugly, brilliant, and real. We built museums for the second and childhoods out of the first.

Treasure Island fixed the pirate image in 1883

blocks.prompt: The Chest We Made Up, and the One We Forgot
blocks.text: There are two treasure chests. One is famous and imaginary. The other is real, and almost nobody can describe it. That gap is worth looking at, because it shows how a good story can bury a better one. Start with the imaginary chest. It has a domed lid, iron bands, and a spill of gold coins. It waits on an island under a palm tree, and a map marks the place with an X. Ask where that picture came from and the trail is surprisingly short. It does not run back to real pirates. It runs back to a wet afternoon in 1881, when Robert Louis Stevenson, stuck indoors in the Scottish Highlands, drew an island to amuse his stepson. He inked the bays, wrote in the names, marked a few crosses for buried gold, and found that the drawing was already suggesting people. As he put it afterward, the characters began to appear among the imaginary woods. He wrote the book to explain the map. Treasure Island issued the modern pirate almost fully assembled: the parrot, the black spot, the one-legged sea cook, pieces of eight, and above all the map. Edgar Allan Poe had already used a coded message and Captain Kidd's buried gold in The Gold-Bug in 1843, so the idea was in the air, but Stevenson is the one who fixed it in place. Every pirate cartoon since has been quoting a Victorian novelist's rainy-day doodle. Real pirates did not bury treasure, and the reason is plain economics. A pirate crew was a short, violent business venture. Loot in a hole cannot be spent, requires you to survive, requires you to find the spot again, and requires your shipmates to be honest, which was not their defining trait. So crews split the takings at once, under written articles that set shares by rank and even paid compensation for lost limbs, and then they spent it in port. The one well-documented burial is Captain William Kidd's, on Gardiners Island in 1699, and it was less a hiding place than a bargaining chip. It failed completely. The governor's men dug it up within months, sent it to London, and spread it across a courtroom as evidence. Kidd was hanged in 1701, and his body was left in an iron cage above the Thames for years as a warning to others. The one pirate who did bury treasure was hanged with the help of it. Now the real chest. In the 1600s, ironworkers in Nuremberg and Augsburg built the best strongboxes in Europe. Dealers today market them as armada chests, a name that suggests salt spray and cannon smoke, though most never saw a harbor. They sat in counting houses, guild halls, and town treasuries, bolted down, holding payroll and paperwork. They are plain, dark, brutally heavy, and their brilliance is hidden. Lift the lid and the entire underside is a machine: one turn of the key drives a dozen or more iron bolts outward into the frame on every side at the same instant. The keyhole on the front, the one your hand goes to first, is a fake. It is a decoy, machined carefully so that a thief will spend his night on it. The true hole sits in the lid, under a flap you must know how to release. Some chests hide a second compartment inside the first. The comparison is not flattering to us. We remember the chest that was buried in a story and forgot the chest that was engineered by people who actually had something to protect. The imaginary one asks nothing of you but a shovel. The real one asks you to understand it. We chose the shovel.
